Question: A and B play sudoku until A has 3 consecutive wins. They know that there are three cases: win, tie, lose and the probability is uniform. What is the expected value of the number of matches that they played?
Answer: Sudoku…?? How’s that a 2-player game? I seem to have missed a memo. Anyway, you’re asking for the expected number of trials until we get 3 successes in a row, where the probability of success is 1 / 3 . At any moment, our state is determined by the number of consecutive recent successes, which can be 0 , 1 or 2 (at 3 we have won). Let E 0 , E 1 and E 2 be the expected number of additional trials we need to get a 3 -peat when we are in each of the states. The relevant transition probabilities are 1 / 3 to move from E 0 to E 1 , from E 1 to E 2 and from E 2 to success, with 2 / 3 taking us back from E 2 to E 0 , E 1 to E 0 and E 0 to itself. Thus we have the equations: E 0 = 2 3 ( 1 + E 0 ) + 1 3 ( 1 + E 1 ) E 1 = 2 3 ( 1 + E 0 ) + 1 3 ( 1 + E 2 ) E 2 = 2 3 ( 1 + E 0 ) + 1 3 ⋅ 1 Solving those linear equations yields E 0 = 39 , E 1 = 36 and E 2 = 27 . The expected number of games, or trials, is 39 . ■ (…)

Answer: The wording of the question is a bit peculiar: there’s no need to require that m be odd. In fact, if m is even then 2 m − 1 doesn’t divide 3 n − 1 ever, regardless of the parity of n . But that’s an easier observation ( 2 m − 1 is divisible by 3 when m is even) so, presumably, the question just wants us to focus on the harder case. The smallest m of interest here is m = 3 , and 2 3 − 1 = 7 . Why can’t 7 divide 3 n − 1 ? Well it sure can, for instance it divides 3 6 − 1 , but it can only do so when n is even, because the order of 3 mod 7 is 6 , meaning 3 n ≡ 1 ( mod 7 ) only when 6 | n . This gives us a starting point: to show that 2 m − 1 can’t divide 3 n − 1 we want a prime p which divides the former and not the latter, and a good way to show that such a p can’t divide 3 n − 1 for odd n is to argue that the order of 3 mod p is even. The order of 3 mod p always divides p − 1 , which is even. If the order is odd then it must actually divide ( p − 1 ) / 2 , which means that 3 ( p − 1 ) / 2 ≡ 1 ( mod p ) , which means that 3 is a quadratic residue mod p , which means that p ≡ ± 1 ( mod 12 ) , by quadratic reciprocity. So, conversely, if p ≡ ± 5 ( mod 12 ) then 3 is not a quadratic residue, so 3 ( p − 1 ) / 2 ≡ − 1 ( mod p ) , and therefore the order of 3 mod p must be even. Finally, we observe that 2 m − 1 is 3 mod 4 and 1 mod 3 when m is odd, so it is 7 mod 12 . A number congruent to 7 mod 12 cannot have all of its prime factors be ± 1 ( mod 12 ) , since the product of such primes is also ± 1 ( mod 12 ) , and we’re done. Question: What do you think about the achievement of Dr. Soberno Isaac Bari received Ph.D in Mathematics from MIT at 16 years old?
Answer: As far as I can tell, Soborno (or Suborno) Isaac Bari is not yet 16 years old, and has not earned a Ph.D. in mathematics. If some teenager earns a Ph.D. in mathematics from MIT, I’m not sure what thoughts I should have about it, or what value my opinions might have. I mean, cool…? The fascination with child prodigies is not particularly helpful or healthy, in my mind. If the person proves something interesting (to me) in their Ph.D. thesis, I’d love to learn about it (Daniel Larsen’s paper is a good example). Answer: This is just a mischievous little trick. Why are they saying that m , n need to be different? Well, because obviously if m = n then m ! m ! is a perfect square (duh). So we’re not allowed to do that, but maybe we can… almost do that? What if n = m + 1 ? Then we are looking at m ! ( m + 1 ) ! . That’s the product of all things up to m , times the product of all things up to m again, times m + 1 . So… m ! ( m + 1 ) ! = ( m ! ) 2 ⋅ ( m + 1 ) Is that a perfect square? Usually not, but it sure is if m + 1 itself is a perfect square! So, our infinitely many pairs are just 3 ! 4 ! , 8 ! 9 ! , 15 ! 16 ! and so on. Incidentally, Erdős proved that the product of any number > 1 of consecutive positive integers is never a perfect square. Consequently, our mischievous infinite sequence of pairs contains all possible solutions of m ! n ! = k 2 with m < n . There are no other solutions. (…)

Question: Why do mathematicians do research on Collatz's conjunctions? What are they going to achieve or gain?
Answer: (It’s the Collatz conjecture.) Here’s a simple syllogism which somehow isn’t sufficiently well-known: People do things for fun, for the sheer joy of it. You could argue that there’s this personal “gain” from such activities (enjoyment), but it’s not the same kind of “gain” you seem to be looking for. You don’t “gain” anything necessarily by going on a hike, reading a novel or playing something on your guitar, but you do this anyway. Fun. (You wouldn’t ask “Why do people have sex? What are they going to achieve or gain?”, would you? Same thing.) Exploring the Collatz conjecture can reasonably be done by a person just because they are intrigued, and they want to walk down a path and see where it leads them. Perfectly normal. Nevertheless, in the context of mathematical research, there are deeper reasons. The Collatz conjecture deals with iterations of a simple map, and exploring such iterations is a beautiful domain of mathematics called dynamical systems. People dedicate entire lives to studying dynamical systems, because they find them fascinating and sometimes useful for making discoveries in other parts of math. (You may now ask, but why do people do research on dynamical systems? What are they going to achieve or gain? This is the same as asking why do people do math research at all, and the answer is because they can’t imagine anything better to do with their lives, and luckily society appreciates that for many good reasons.) So, people may explore the Collatz iteration as a toy example to better understand something more general that they are thinking about. We study toy examples all the time. We can’t solve the very general problem of classifying the orbits of arbitrary maps on arbitrary spaces, so we’re looking for simpler problems we could possibly solve, and Collatz is one of the seemingly simplest ones. As an example, let’s read carefully what is perhaps the most recent major paper on the Collatz conjecture, Terry Tao’s Almost all orbits. In the paper you find a whole lot of subtle analysis of the Collatz map, but you also find things like Nevertheless, in this paper we show that it is possible to locate an alternate probability measure (or more precisely, a family of probability measures) on the natural numbers with enough invariance properties that an iterative argument does become fruitful. and In this analogy, Theorem 1.6 then corresponds to an “almost sure almost global well-posedness” result, where one needs to control the solution for times so large that the evolution gets arbitrary close to the bounded state N = O ( 1 ) . To bootstrap from almost sure local well-posedness to almost sure almost global well-posedness, we were inspired by the work of Bourgain [4], who demonstrated an almost sure global well-posedness result for a certain nonlinear Schrödinger equation by combining local well-posedness theory with a construction of an invariant probability measure for the dynamics. Roughly speaking, the point was that the invariance of the measure would almost surely keep the solution in a “bounded” region of the state space for arbitrarily long times, allowing one to iterate the local well-posedness theory indefinitely. What these two brief quotes tell you is that Tao’s study of Collatz isn’t an isolated, random pastime. He is connecting it with broader ideas of invariant measures for dynamical systems and PDEs. Much of math research seeks to find connections between diverse areas, elucidating or harnessing them in different directions. So, bottom line: there are some serious motivations for studying the Collatz conjecture as a useful sandbox for ideas about dynamical systems, invariance and local-global principles, but it is also fine to study the Collatz conjecture just because it is there, and it’s interesting, and it’s fun. That’s all. (…)
